newsitem.title: UK: Still work to be done on financial supervision - BoE.
newsitem.headline: Still work to be done on financial supervision - BoE.

text.p: Better supervision of large financial groups would significantly reduce the risk of a major mishap in one part having an adverse effect on the rest of the group, a senior Bank of England official said on Wednesday.

Michael Foot, head of supervision and surveillance at the Bank of England, told a conference on systemic risk "there is as yet no agreed basis for the consolidated supervision of a group spanning insurance, banking and securities".

This also applies to "the limited number but important set of U.S. investment banks which contain large entities which are effectively unregulated either in their own right or on a consolidated basis," Foot said.

"Although we have gone a long way towards a better understanding of how a financial group should be supervised on a consolidated basis as well as within its component parts, there is still much more to be done," Foot said.
But the issue is at the forefront of regulators' minds.

"With the active co-operation of some of the world's largest financial conglomerates and with the involvement of insurance, banking and securities supervisors from a wide range of countries - this issue is very much on the front burner," Foot said in his speech to the conference.
Foot said the prize for success "would be a significant reduction in the risk of an adverse shock in one part of a financial conglomerate spilling over unnecessarily into the rest of the group".

Recent financial disasters such as the collapse of Britain's Barings Bank in 1995 and trading losses at Daiwa Bank in New York had, Foot said, resulted in greater willingness to share information across regulatory and geographical borders.
"The challenge is to ensure the sharing of relevant information on a timely basis between regulators willing and able to act together," Foot said.
Information sharing could only take place effectively if the regulators were clear about their respective responsibilities, in normal circumstances and in times of crisis, he added.
Foot said the threat of so-called "systemic risk", where a problem in one area can trigger a meltdown in the whole system, appeared to have lessened over the last 20 years.

"The structural development of financial markets in recent years has increased the chances of ripple effects spreading from one market to another but correspondingly reduced the risk of those being serious waves rather than ripples," he said, adding that a central banker he "wouldn't want to bet the family silver on that conclusion".
